questions.stem: Which change best explains why people now tend to work in teams more than individually?
options: the growth of service industries in the second half of the 20th century
the decline of all manufacturing work since the Industrial Revolution began
laws passed in the 20th century that banned working on tasks alone
the disappearance of any need for specialised skills at work
questions.explanation: Changes in working conditions since the Industrial Revolution, especially the rise of service industries, created complex work that needs people with different skills to cooperate.

questions.stem: Which factor is most important for a team to optimise its performance and achieve common goals?
options: clear shared goals that all members understand
members working separately so they do not disagree
one member making every decision without input
keeping information within each member's own role
questions.explanation: Teams perform best with clear common goals, defined roles, open communication and trust. Working in isolation or hoarding information undermines the benefits of teamwork.

questions.stem: A hospital forms a team of doctors, nurses, physiotherapists and social workers to plan patients' discharge. What is the main advantage of this interdisciplinary team?
options: It guarantees that no conflict will ever occur
It combines expertise to solve complex problems
It ensures that every member has identical skills
It removes the need for communication between members
questions.explanation: Interdisciplinary teams bring complementary knowledge to complex tasks. However, different professional languages and priorities can create communication and conflict challenges.

questions.stem: Belbin's team roles describe:
options: the levels of an organisation's culture from visible to hidden
the ways people tend to behave and contribute within a team
the official job titles listed in an organisation's structure
the stages a team passes through as it develops over time
questions.explanation: Belbin identified nine team roles, clusters of behaviour such as Plant, Shaper and Completer Finisher, that people tend to adopt. Effective teams have a balance of roles.

questions.stem: In Belbin's model, a team member who generates creative ideas and solves difficult problems in unconventional ways is the:
options: Plant
Completer Finisher
Implementer
Teamworker
questions.explanation: The Plant is creative and imaginative. The Completer Finisher polishes and checks work for errors, the Implementer turns ideas into practical action, and the Teamworker supports cooperation.

questions.stem: A team has many members who generate ideas but none who check details or meet deadlines. Using Belbin's model, which role is the team most likely missing?
options: Completer Finisher
Plant
Resource Investigator
Shaper
questions.explanation: The Completer Finisher pays close attention to detail and makes sure work is finished on time and to a high standard. A team of idea generators risks never finishing tasks.

questions.stem: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator classifies people into types using four pairs of preferences. Which is one of these pairs?
options: existence and growth
expectancy and valence of rewards
extraversion and introversion
honesty and humility
questions.explanation: The Myers-Briggs uses extraversion-introversion, sensing-intuition, thinking-feeling and judging-perceiving, giving 16 types. The other pairs come from HEXACO, Alderfer and Vroom.

questions.stem: An organisation uses Myers-Briggs results to decide who is allowed to join project teams. Why would an organisational psychologist advise against this?
options: It measures intelligence, which is irrelevant to working in a team
It produces too many types, so no two employees could ever work together
It can only be completed by people who already have a leadership role
Its types are often unstable on retesting and predict performance poorly
questions.explanation: The Myers-Briggs can prompt useful discussion of preferences, but many people receive a different type on retesting and it has limited evidence for predicting performance, so it should not be used for selection decisions.

questions.stem: Groupthink occurs when:
options: group members work harder because their individual efforts are noticed
a team's leader changes style depending on the members' readiness
a wish for harmony leads a group to decide poorly without debate
a group reaches a better decision by considering many viewpoints
questions.explanation: Groupthink is faulty decision-making in a cohesive group where members suppress doubts to maintain agreement. Alternatives are not properly considered.

questions.stem: Which is a symptom of groupthink?
options: members censoring their doubts to avoid conflict
members openly inviting criticism of the plan
a leader asking an outsider to review the decision
the group splitting into smaller groups to debate
questions.explanation: Symptoms include self-censorship, an illusion of unanimity, pressure on dissenters and a sense of invulnerability. Inviting criticism and outside review are ways to prevent groupthink.

questions.stem: Which strategy would best reduce the risk of groupthink in a management team?
options: requiring decisions to be made quickly and unanimously
appointing someone to argue against the preferred option
having the leader state a preferred option at the start
making the team more isolated from outside opinions
questions.explanation: A devil's advocate, inviting outside experts and leaders withholding their views early encourage critical evaluation. A leader stating a preference early and pressure for fast unanimity increase groupthink.

questions.stem: How can workplace bullying affect team performance?
options: It improves performance by pushing members to work harder
It affects only the person targeted and not the rest of the team
It increases communication because members discuss it often
It lowers trust and wellbeing, so cooperation suffers
questions.explanation: Bullying damages the target's wellbeing and creates fear and mistrust among others, leading to absenteeism, turnover and poorer teamwork.

questions.stem: A team agrees that everyone will be allowed to finish speaking in meetings without interruption. This is an example of:
options: a Belbin team role
a norm of interaction
groupthink
a hygiene factor
questions.explanation: Norms of interaction are the shared expectations about how team members communicate and behave with one another. Positive norms support respectful, effective teamwork.

questions.stem: Reciprocal engagement in a team refers to:
options: a leader giving orders that members carry out without question
members actively contributing and responding to each other
one member doing most of the work while others watch
members exchanging gifts to build loyalty to the leader
questions.explanation: In reciprocal engagement, all members participate and respond to each other's contributions, which builds shared understanding and commitment.

questions.stem: A virtual team spread across three countries communicates only by email and has frequent misunderstandings. Which change would most likely improve its performance?
options: reducing all communication so members can focus on their own tasks
removing all deadlines so that time differences no longer matter
assigning all decisions to the most senior member to save time
adding regular video meetings for richer, real-time contact
questions.explanation: Email lacks tone and immediate feedback, so misunderstandings are common. Richer forms of communication, such as video, provide non-verbal cues and allow quick clarification.

questions.stem: In Tuckman and Jensen's stages of team development, which stage involves conflict as members challenge ideas and compete for roles?
options: performing
storming
forming
norming
questions.explanation: In the storming stage, members express differences and may clash over roles and approaches. Forming is the polite, uncertain start; norming is when shared rules develop; performing is when the team works effectively.

questions.stem: Information processing theory can be used to understand team communication. Which statement fits this approach?
options: Messages are encoded and decoded, and noise can distort them
Communication depends only on the personality of the team leader
Teams communicate best when they receive as much information as possible
Messages are always understood exactly as the sender intended
questions.explanation: An information processing view treats communication as encoding, transmitting and decoding messages. Distractions, unclear messages and information overload can cause misunderstanding, so communication should be clear and manageable.

questions.stem: In the Thomas-Kilmann model, conflict-management styles are classified by which two dimensions?
options: extraversion and introversion
assertiveness and cooperativeness
task and relationship behaviour of the leader
expectancy and instrumentality
questions.explanation: The model places five styles according to how assertive (concerned with one's own needs) and how cooperative (concerned with others' needs) a person is. Task and relationship behaviour belong to Hersey and Blanchard's leadership model.

questions.stem: Two team members work together to find a solution that fully meets both of their needs. Which conflict-management style is this?
options: accommodating
avoiding
collaborating
compromising
questions.explanation: Collaborating is high in both assertiveness and cooperativeness and aims for a solution that satisfies everyone. Compromising involves each side giving up something.

questions.stem: A team member always gives in to others' wishes to keep the peace, even when she disagrees. Which conflict-management style is she using?
options: compromising
accommodating
competing
collaborating
questions.explanation: Accommodating is low in assertiveness and high in cooperativeness: the person puts others' concerns ahead of their own. Competing is the opposite.

questions.stem: Why might it help a team if its members complete a measure of conflict-management styles?
options: It prevents all conflict from arising within the team in future
Members can see their usual styles and choose more suitable ones
It allows the leader to remove members with any competing style
It shows which single style should be used in every situation
questions.explanation: Knowing their preferred styles helps members understand reactions in conflict and adapt. Each style suits some situations, so no single style is always best.

questions.stem: The trait theory of leadership proposes that:
options: effective leadership depends mainly on the situation
anyone can lead well if given enough authority
leaders should adapt their style to each follower
effective leaders have certain personal characteristics
questions.explanation: Trait theory assumes good leaders are born with or possess traits such as confidence, intelligence and integrity. Contingency theories argue that effective leadership depends on the situation.

questions.stem: What is a main criticism of trait theories of leadership?
options: They pay too much attention to the readiness of followers in different situations
They claim leadership is learned entirely through operant conditioning at work
They propose that leaders should always delegate decisions to their teams
No set of traits consistently predicts effective leadership in every situation
questions.explanation: Research has found that traits linked with leadership in one context do not always predict success in another, and trait theory ignores the influence of followers and situations.

questions.stem: According to Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership theory, effective leadership depends mainly on:
options: matching the leader's style to the followers' readiness
the leader having inborn traits such as charisma
the organisation's profit in the previous financial year
the leader using the same style with every follower
questions.explanation: Hersey and Blanchard's contingency theory proposes that leaders should vary their amount of task and relationship behaviour to suit how able and willing followers are to do the task.

questions.stem: A new apprentice is keen but has no experience of the task. Using Hersey and Blanchard's model, which style is most appropriate?
options: telling, with clear instructions and close supervision
delegating, by giving the apprentice full responsibility
participating, by sharing decisions as an equal colleague
avoiding, by letting the apprentice learn by trial and error
questions.explanation: When readiness is low, followers need high task direction, which is the telling style. Delegating suits followers who are both able and willing.

questions.stem: An experienced, confident team member is highly skilled and motivated. Which Hersey and Blanchard style best suits her?
options: selling
close directing
delegating
telling
questions.explanation: High readiness means the follower is able and willing, so the leader can hand over responsibility with little task or relationship input. Telling suits low readiness.

questions.stem: How does Hersey and Blanchard's theory differ from trait theory in what it assumes is critical to leadership?
options: It argues that one style is best for every team
It emphasises the situation and followers, not fixed personal qualities
It emphasises fixed personal qualities, not the situation and followers
It argues that leaders are born rather than trained
questions.explanation: Trait theory locates effective leadership in the leader's characteristics, while contingency theories such as Hersey and Blanchard's argue that the best style depends on the circumstances, so leadership can be learned.

questions.stem: According to Schein, what are the three levels of organisational culture?
options: hygiene factors, motivators and job satisfaction
artefacts, espoused values and basic assumptions
artefacts, team roles and conflict-management styles
skill variety, task identity and task significance
questions.explanation: Schein described visible artefacts, espoused beliefs and values, and basic underlying assumptions that are taken for granted and largely unconscious.

questions.stem: A company's office layout, dress code and logo belong to which level of Schein's model?
options: basic underlying assumptions
subcultures
artefacts
espoused values
questions.explanation: Artefacts are the visible, tangible features of an organisation, such as buildings, dress, language and rituals. They are easy to see but can be hard to interpret.

questions.stem: A company's mission statement says it values work-life balance, but staff who leave on time are seen as uncommitted. In Schein's terms, this shows:
options: that espoused values are always the deepest level of culture
a gap between espoused values and basic underlying assumptions
agreement between artefacts and basic underlying assumptions
that the company has no organisational culture at all
questions.explanation: Espoused values are what the organisation says it believes; basic assumptions are the deeper, taken-for-granted beliefs that actually drive behaviour. Here the assumption that long hours show commitment contradicts the stated value.

questions.stem: What is the difference between organisational culture and organisational climate?
options: Culture applies to government bodies; climate applies to commercial businesses
Culture and climate are two names for exactly the same thing
Culture is deep shared assumptions; climate is shared perceptions of the current work environment
Climate is deep shared assumptions; culture is shared perceptions of the current work environment
questions.explanation: Culture refers to the deep values and assumptions that develop over time. Climate is how employees currently perceive the work environment, such as how safe or supportive it feels, and can change more quickly.

questions.stem: In a hospital, nurses, surgeons and administrative staff have different shared norms and ways of working. These groups are examples of:
options: Belbin's team roles
conflict-management styles
leadership styles
organisational subcultures
questions.explanation: Subcultures form within an organisation around departments, job types, age or other groupings. They can enrich an organisation but may also create conflict if their values clash.

questions.stem: A factory measures how workers perceive management's commitment to safety. Which concept is being assessed?
options: the organisation's artefacts
the workers' Holland codes
the workers' team roles
the organisation's safety climate
questions.explanation: Measures such as safety climate questionnaires assess employees' shared perceptions of policies and practices. A positive safety climate is linked to fewer accidents.

questions.stem: How can organisational culture and climate affect organisational performance?
options: Performance is decided only by pay, so culture is not a factor
A supportive culture can raise satisfaction and cut turnover
Culture and climate affect only managers, not other employees
A strong culture always guarantees high profits in every industry
questions.explanation: When values and practices support employees, satisfaction, commitment and cooperation tend to rise and turnover falls. Culture can also hinder performance if it resists change.

questions.stem: An organisational psychologist is asked to help a company improve its culture. What is a sensible first step?
options: copy the culture of the most profitable company in the country
change the logo and office colours to signal a new culture
measure the current culture and the gap with the desired one
replace all senior managers before collecting any data
questions.explanation: An evidence-based approach starts by assessing the existing culture, for example with a culture-gap survey, to identify what needs to change. Changing artefacts alone rarely changes deeper assumptions.

questions.stem: Which task is typical of the work of an organisational psychologist?
options: designing selection processes and improving teamwork
prescribing medication to employees with mental illness
auditing the organisation's financial accounts each year
writing the legal contracts for new employees
questions.explanation: Organisational psychologists work on selection, training, motivation, teamwork, leadership, culture and wellbeing at work. Prescribing medication, auditing and legal drafting are done by other professionals.
